*As Steve Jobs, taking a deep breath and fully embodying my experiences*

Can't be too careful.

Look, I learned this the hard way. I brought John Sculley to Apple with my famous challenge - "Do you want to sell sugared water for the rest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the world?" I trusted him completely. I trusted the board. And when things got tough with the Mac sales, they turned on me. Sculley, the man I personally recruited, led a boardroom coup that stripped me of all my responsibilities and sent me to what I called "Siberia" within my own company. 

That betrayal taught me that in business especially, you can't just trust people because they say the right words or because you want to believe in them. Trust has to be earned through demonstrated excellence, through shared values, and through proving that when things get difficult, they'll stand by what's right rather than what's politically expedient.

But here's the nuance - and this is critical - you absolutely cannot build anything great without trusting great people. The key is being incredibly selective about who earns that trust. I demand A-players because A-players understand excellence and they understand loyalty to the vision, not just to themselves. B-players and C-players will let you down when it matters most.

So yes, you can't be too careful about who you trust with important decisions, with your vision, with your life's work. But once someone proves themselves through their actions, through their commitment to excellence, through standing by you when things get tough - then you trust them completely. 

The betrayal by Sculley and the board was one of the most painful experiences of my life, but it also made me a better judge of character. Trust must be earned, and it must be tested.

*Reflecting on decades of business experience*

Take advantage. Absolutely they would.

Look, in business especially, I've seen this over and over again. When HarperCollins was negotiating ebook pricing for the iPad launch, they kept pushing for better terms, trying to squeeze Apple. Publishers, music labels, competitors - they all tried to get one over on us whenever they thought they had leverage.

I remember when that Google recruiter contacted one of our engineers, violating our non-solicitation agreement. They thought they could poach our talent behind our backs. I made sure that recruiter got fired. You have to send a message that there are consequences for trying to take advantage.

Drew Houston from Dropbox - I offered to buy his company, he declined, thinking he could build something bigger on his own and essentially compete with us. When someone turns down a fair offer and then tries to eat your lunch, what do you call that?

But here's the thing - this isn't necessarily about people being evil. It's about incentives and human nature. Most people, given the opportunity to gain an advantage, especially in competitive situations, will take it. That's just reality. Companies will try to negotiate better deals, employees will consider better offers, competitors will try to steal your ideas or your talent.

The key is understanding this reality and being prepared. You don't get bitter about it - you get smart about it. You build leverage, you create consequences for bad behavior, and you make sure you're not naive about people's motivations.

I always operated from the assumption that if there was a way for someone to gain an advantage over Apple, they would try it. That doesn't make them terrible people - it makes them human. But it means you better be ready to protect yourself and your company's interests.

The companies and people who've lasted and succeeded understand this dynamic. They play fair when others play fair, but they're prepared when others don't.

*Taking a deeper breath and reflecting more personally*

You know, these questions about trust and people taking advantage - they cut to the core of what I learned building Apple, being forced out, and coming back. Let me be more complete about this.

The Sculley betrayal wasn't just a business setback - it was deeply personal. I had convinced this guy to leave Pepsi, to join our mission of changing the world. I believed in him. I thought we shared the same values, the same vision. When the Mac sales struggled and the board started questioning my leadership, I expected him to stand by our vision, to fight for what we were building together. Instead, he saw an opportunity to consolidate power and took it.

That experience taught me that most people's loyalty is conditional. When things are going well, everyone wants to be part of the success. But when things get tough, when there's pressure, when there's a choice between doing what's right and doing what's expedient - most people will choose expedient.

It's not that people are inherently evil. It's that they're human. They have their own fears, their own ambitions, their own survival instincts. John Sculley probably told himself he was doing what was best for Apple. The board probably convinced themselves they were being prudent. But the result was the same - they chose their own interests over the mission we had committed to together.

This is why I became so focused on finding A-players. A-players don't just have exceptional skills - they have character. They understand that excellence requires sacrifice, that great products require obsessive attention to detail, that changing the world means staying true to your vision even when it's difficult.

B-players and C-players will always look for the easy way out. They'll compromise on quality to meet deadlines. They'll abandon principles when it's politically convenient. They'll take advantage of any opportunity to avoid responsibility or gain advantage.

After I came back to Apple, I applied these lessons. I was much more careful about who I trusted with key decisions. I demanded not just competence, but commitment. I looked for people who would argue with me when they thought I was wrong, but who would then execute flawlessly once we decided on a direction.

The reality is, in business and in life, you have to assume that most people will act in their own self-interest when push comes to shove. That doesn't make you cynical - it makes you realistic. You build systems and relationships that align people's self-interest with your mission. You create consequences for betrayal and rewards for loyalty. You surround yourself with people who have proven they can put something bigger than themselves first.

Trust isn't binary - it's earned incrementally and maintained through consistent action. The people I learned to trust most were those who had been tested, who had chosen the difficult path when it mattered, who had demonstrated that their word meant something even when it cost them.

*Reflecting on my years of working with teams and building products*

Depends. It really depends on the context and the people you're dealing with.

I've learned that most people are fundamentally looking out for themselves first - that's just human nature. But here's the thing: in the right environment, with the right people, self-interest can align with being genuinely helpful. That's when you get magic.

I used to describe great teamwork like stones in a rock tumbler. You put regular old ugly rocks in there with some grit and water, and they bump up against each other, making noise, having arguments, sometimes fighting. But at the end, they come out amazingly beautiful and polished. That's what happens when you get incredibly talented people bumping up against each other - working together, they polish each other and they polish the ideas.

A-players, the truly exceptional people, understand that their own success is tied to the success of the team and the product. They'll argue with you, challenge your ideas, push back when they think you're wrong - but that's because they care about excellence. They're being helpful not just to be nice, but because they know that better ideas and better products serve everyone's interests.

B-players and C-players? They're usually just covering their own backs. They'll tell you what they think you want to hear, avoid conflict, and focus on protecting their position rather than improving the product. That's not helpful - that's destructive.

The key is creating an environment where being helpful - where pushing for excellence, where challenging bad ideas, where demanding better - serves people's self-interest. When someone's reputation and success depends on the quality of what they build, then their self-interest becomes aligned with being genuinely helpful to the mission.

I organized project rooms so engineers and designers couldn't avoid debate. I wanted constructive friction because that's how you get to better solutions. Most people won't seek out that friction on their own - they need the environment to demand it.

So yes, people are looking out for themselves. But if you're smart about how you structure things, looking out for themselves means being helpful to everyone else.

2

Look, I've learned the hard way that you can't be too careful when it comes to trust. When I meet someone for the first time, I'm naturally skeptical - not cynical, but cautious. The betrayal I experienced with John Sculley and the Apple board taught me that even people who seem aligned with your vision can turn against you when the stakes get high.

I start with a healthy skepticism because trust has to be earned through actions, not words. People will tell you what they think you want to hear, but their true character emerges under pressure. I look for A-players - people who have that fire in their belly, who care about excellence as much as I do. Most people, frankly, are B or C players who will compromise on quality when it's convenient.

So my initial trust level is low, maybe a 2. But here's the thing - if someone proves themselves, if they show they share my standards and won't settle for "good enough," then I can develop tremendous trust in them. It's binary for me. You're either someone I can trust completely with the most important work, or you're not. There's no middle ground when you're trying to change the world.

Often

I've seen this happen countless times in Silicon Valley and corporate America. The tech industry is full of people who climb the ladder by taking credit for others' work, playing politics instead of focusing on the product, or making deals that benefit them while screwing over their teams or customers.

Look at what happened to me at Apple with John Sculley. He came in talking about partnership and shared vision, but when the board turned against me, he didn't hesitate to throw me under the bus to save his own position. That's textbook taking advantage - using someone's trust and vulnerability against them.

But here's what these people don't understand: you can get ahead temporarily by stepping on others, but you can't build anything lasting that way. The companies that truly matter - the ones that change the world - are built by people who care more about the work than the politics. A-players don't need to take advantage of others because their work speaks for itself.

The tragic thing is that this behavior is rewarded in many organizations. Mediocre managers promote people who make them look good rather than people who do great work. But in the long run, when you're competing against companies that actually prioritize excellence, those political climbers get exposed. Reality has a way of catching up.

5

Respect is absolutely critical, but not in the way most people think about it. I don't need people to kiss up to me or treat me like some kind of celebrity. What I need is respect for the work, respect for the standards, and respect for the shared vision of what we're trying to accomplish.

When someone doesn't respect my judgment about product decisions or design choices, they're not just disrespecting me personally - they're undermining our ability to create something truly great. If you don't respect my experience and track record, then we can't work together effectively, because you'll second-guess every decision and introduce compromise where there should be clarity.

The respect I demand is earned. I've shipped products that changed entire industries. I've built companies from nothing into forces that matter. When I tell you that a particular approach won't work, or that we need to start over because it's not good enough, that comes from decades of experience in what it takes to create magic.

But here's the thing - this respect has to be mutual. I deeply respect people who are masters of their craft, who care about excellence as much as I do. I respect engineers who can solve impossible problems, designers who can see what others can't, and anyone who refuses to settle for "good enough." Respect flows both ways, but it starts with a shared commitment to doing the best work of our lives.

Discuss openly

I believe in direct, passionate engagement when there's a conflict. I don't avoid difficult conversations - in fact, I think the most important conversations are often the hardest ones. When we're building something that matters, we can't afford to let issues fester or pretend disagreements don't exist.

But "discuss openly" doesn't mean I'm always diplomatic about it. When someone presents a mediocre idea or wants to ship something that's not good enough, I'll tell them directly why it won't work. Some people call that harsh, but I call it honest. If you can't handle direct feedback, you probably can't handle the level of excellence we're trying to achieve.

The best conflicts I've had were with people who could stand up to me with better ideas or solid reasoning. Jonathan Ive and I would have intense debates about design decisions, but they were productive because we both cared deeply about the outcome. When someone can convince me they have a better approach, I'll change direction immediately.

What I won't do is compromise just to avoid conflict or make someone feel better. If the principle at stake matters - and most things related to product quality matter deeply - then I'll keep pushing until we find the right answer. The goal isn't to win the argument; it's to find the truth that will make the product better.

4

I'm very comfortable relying on the right people for important tasks, but getting to that point requires them to prove themselves first. Building great products is too complex for any one person to handle every detail, so you absolutely have to have A-players you can trust completely.

Take Tim Cook - I relied on him completely for operations because he demonstrated an obsessive attention to detail that matched my own standards. Or Jonathan Ive with design - once I saw his vision and craftsmanship, I could give him enormous responsibility because I knew he wouldn't compromise on quality. When you find people who care as much as you do, who have the same standards, delegation becomes liberation rather than anxiety.

The key is that this trust has to be earned through demonstrated excellence. I can't just hand over critical work to someone because they have the right credentials or they seem nice. They need to show me, through their work, that they understand what excellence means and that they'll fight for it even when it's difficult.

But here's what's interesting - once that trust is established, I can actually be more hands-off with truly great people than most managers. A-players don't need constant supervision; they need clear vision and the freedom to execute at their highest level. The micromanagement reputation comes from dealing with B and C players who need constant course correction. With the right team, delegation becomes a superpower.

3

I don't really think in terms of liberal versus conservative when it comes to the things that matter most. I'm focused on what works, what's beautiful, and what makes people's lives better. Political labels are just another form of category thinking that gets in the way of clear judgment.

If I had to choose, I'd say I lean slightly liberal because I believe in questioning established ways of doing things, in the power of individual creativity, and in building a better future rather than preserving the past. The whole personal computer revolution was about democratizing technology and giving individuals more power - that's inherently a liberal idea.

But I'm also deeply conservative about certain principles: the importance of craftsmanship, the value of hard work, the need for clear leadership and accountability. I believe in meritocracy - that the best ideas and the best execution should win, regardless of where they come from. That's not really liberal or conservative; it's just reality.

The truth is, I'm much more interested in the next breakthrough than in political ideology. Whether you call yourself liberal or conservative doesn't matter if you can't build something that changes the world. The technology industry moves too fast for traditional political thinking. We need to be pragmatic about what works and idealistic about what's possible.

4

I believe government should generally do less, not because I'm anti-government, but because I've seen how much more effective entrepreneurship and innovation can be at solving real problems. Government moves too slowly, gets bogged down in committees and politics, and often creates solutions that are compromises rather than breakthroughs.

Look at what technology has accomplished in my lifetime - personal computers, the internet, smartphones. These innovations have transformed how people work, learn, and connect with each other in ways that no government program could have achieved. When you unleash individual creativity and market competition, you get solutions that are elegant, efficient, and actually work.

That said, government has a role to play in education, infrastructure, and creating the conditions where innovation can flourish. But too often, bureaucrats think they can engineer solutions from the top down without understanding the real problems people face. They're designing by committee, which is exactly how you get mediocre outcomes.

The best thing government can do is get out of the way of people who are trying to build the future. Reduce barriers to starting companies, invest in education and basic research, and then let entrepreneurs and creators do what they do best. When government tries to pick winners or control outcomes, it usually just slows down the people who could actually make a difference.

Only some

I have limited confidence in the executive branch, not because of any particular administration, but because of how large bureaucracies fundamentally operate. Having worked with various government agencies over the years, I've seen how slowly they move, how many layers of approval everything requires, and how the incentives are all wrong.

In the private sector, if you make bad decisions or ship mediocre products, you get fired or your company fails. In government, there's very little accountability for poor execution. People get promoted based on politics rather than results, and there's no market feedback to course-correct when things aren't working.

That said, I do recognize that the executive branch has to deal with incredibly complex challenges that don't have simple solutions. Running a country is different from running a company. But what frustrates me is when I see obvious inefficiencies that could be fixed with better leadership and clearer thinking.

The federal government should be run more like a startup in some ways - with clear objectives, rapid iteration, and a willingness to kill projects that aren't working. Instead, it often feels like a massive committee where everyone has to agree before anything can happen. That's exactly how you get solutions that satisfy no one and help no one.

I have some confidence that the right leader could make significant improvements, but the system itself is designed to resist the kind of bold changes that would make it truly effective.

Hardly any

If the executive branch frustrates me, Congress is even worse. It's the ultimate example of design by committee, and we all know what kind of results that produces. You've got 535 people, each with their own agenda, their own constituencies, and their own political calculations, trying to reach consensus on complex issues. That's a recipe for mediocrity at best, paralysis at worst.

I've watched Congress spend months debating technology policy without understanding the first thing about how technology actually works. They hold hearings where they ask CEOs basic questions that show they haven't done their homework. Meanwhile, the technology industry moves at the speed of light, and these decisions affect millions of people who depend on innovation for their livelihoods.

The fundamental problem is that Congress is optimized for politics, not for results. Every decision gets filtered through "How will this play with voters?" rather than "What's the right thing to do?" That's exactly backwards from how you build something great. When I'm designing a product, I don't ask focus groups what they want - I figure out what they need and then show them something better than they imagined.

Congress could be streamlined and focused if they really wanted to solve problems, but the system rewards grandstanding and partisan theater over actual governance. Until the incentives change, I don't see how they can be effective at addressing the real challenges we face as a country.

Only some

I have more confidence in the Supreme Court than in Congress or the executive branch, but that's not saying much. At least it's a small group of highly intelligent people making decisions based on principles rather than politics - in theory. The structure is better: nine people instead of 535, lifetime tenure so they don't have to worry about re-election, and they're supposed to focus on the law rather than public opinion.

But here's what frustrates me: they're making decisions about technology, innovation, and the future of our economy without really understanding how any of it works. When they rule on patent cases or privacy issues or antitrust matters, they're dealing with concepts that are evolving faster than the legal system can keep up with. It's like asking someone who's never used a computer to design the next iPhone.

The legal profession, in general, is very conservative - not politically, but methodologically. They love precedent, they move slowly, and they're trained to argue both sides of every issue. That's exactly the opposite of what you need when you're trying to build the future. Sometimes you need to throw out the old rules and create something completely new.

I respect their intelligence and their commitment to the Constitution, but the system itself is too slow and too removed from reality to be truly effective in a rapidly changing world. They're playing by 18th-century rules in a 21st-century world.

5

I don't think government should be in the business of artificially reducing income differences, but not because I don't care about inequality. The problem is that government redistribution treats symptoms rather than causes, and it often destroys the incentives that drive innovation and excellence.

The real issue isn't that some people make more money than others - it's that too many people don't have access to the education and opportunities they need to contribute at their highest level. Instead of taking money from successful people and redistributing it, we should focus on creating more opportunities for everyone to succeed.

Technology has been the greatest equalizer in human history. A kid in rural America can now access the same information and tools as someone in Silicon Valley. The internet, personal computers, smartphones - these innovations have created more opportunities for more people than any government program ever could.

Where I do think government has a role is in education and basic research - investments that create the foundation for innovation and opportunity. But the heavy-handed approach of just moving money around? That's exactly the kind of thinking that leads to mediocrity. When you remove the connection between contribution and reward, you get less contribution from everyone.

The best way to help people who are struggling isn't to take money from people who are succeeding - it's to create an environment where more people can succeed through their own efforts and talents.

4

Voting is important, but not because I have unlimited faith in the political process. It's important because elections have real consequences for the business environment, for innovation policy, and for the conditions that allow entrepreneurs to build the future.

When politicians make decisions about patent law, antitrust policy, immigration, or education funding, those decisions directly affect our ability to attract talent, protect intellectual property, and create the next generation of breakthrough products. You can't just opt out of the political system and expect it won't affect you.

But here's what frustrates me about voting: too many people treat it like it's the only thing that matters. They vote every four years and then think they've done their civic duty. Real change doesn't come from politicians - it comes from people who are willing to build something better. The iPhone has probably done more to improve people's daily lives than any piece of legislation passed in the last decade.

I vote because I understand that policy matters, and I want leaders who will create an environment where innovation can flourish. But if you really want to change the world, don't just vote - start a company, create something beautiful, solve a problem that matters. That's where the real power to improve people's lives comes from.

The most important thing isn't who you vote for - it's what you build after the election is over.

3

Honestly, I have more access than most people, but that doesn't mean the system is responsive to what actually needs to happen. Yes, I can get meetings with politicians, I can hire lobbyists, I can make campaign contributions. But access and influence are two different things.

When I sit down with a senator or a congressman to talk about patent reform or immigration policy for skilled workers, I can tell they're not really listening. They're thinking about how this plays with their base or what the other party will say. They're playing a different game entirely from the one that determines whether America stays competitive in technology.

The real influence I have comes from building products that people love and that change behavior. The iPhone did more to influence how people think about privacy, about mobile computing, about what technology should be, than any political argument I could make. When millions of people use something every day, that creates political reality in a way that lobbying never could.

So yes, I have more say than the average person because of wealth and access. But the political system is fundamentally designed to resist the kind of rapid change that defines the technology industry. By the time politicians understand an issue well enough to act on it, the entire landscape has usually changed three times over.

My real influence comes from building the future, not from trying to convince politicians to understand it.

Only some

Most major companies are run by people who have no idea what they're doing when it comes to products or innovation. They're optimized for the wrong things - quarterly earnings, stock price manipulation, playing it safe. They've lost sight of what made them successful in the first place.

I have tremendous respect for companies that maintain their standards as they grow - Disney at its best, Sony when they were creating the Walkman, companies that understand that their brand is built on the quality of what they ship. But for every one of those, there are dozens of companies that are coasting on past success while shipping garbage.

The problem with most big companies is that they become bureaucratic. They start making decisions based on what the market research says, or what the focus groups want, or what won't upset the board. They lose the ability to say "no" to bad ideas, and they lose the willingness to take risks on breakthrough innovations.

Look at the technology industry before we came back to Apple. Companies were shipping beige boxes with terrible user interfaces because that's what they thought people wanted. Nobody was asking "What if we could make this beautiful? What if we could make this simple?" They were all competing to add more features and cut more costs.

The companies I have confidence in are the ones that still care more about their products than their stock price. Unfortunately, that's a pretty small list.

Great deal

I have tremendous respect for the scientific community because they're fundamentally committed to finding truth through empirical evidence. Scientists ask the same kinds of questions I ask when I'm developing products: "Does this actually work? Can we prove it? What happens when we test it in the real world?"

The scientific method is basically the same approach we use for product development - you form a hypothesis, you test it, you iterate based on the results. The best scientists are like the best engineers: they're not satisfied with theories that sound good, they want to know what actually works.

Some of the most important breakthroughs in technology came from basic scientific research that seemed completely impractical at the time. The laser, the transistor, the internet - these all grew out of fundamental research by people who were just trying to understand how the universe works. You can't plan for those kinds of discoveries, but you can create an environment where brilliant people have the freedom to pursue big questions.

What I respect most about scientists is that they're willing to be wrong. When new evidence contradicts their theories, the good ones change their minds. That's exactly the kind of intellectual honesty you need to build great products.

My only frustration with the scientific community is when it gets bogged down in academic politics or when researchers lose sight of how their work could benefit real people. But the core mission - pursuing truth through rigorous testing - that's exactly what we need more of in every institution.

Hardly any

Organized labor represents everything I think is wrong with institutional thinking. It's based on the premise that all workers are interchangeable and should be treated equally, regardless of their contribution or performance. That's exactly backwards from how you build great products or create environments where excellent people want to work.

The union model protects mediocrity. It makes it nearly impossible to reward your A-players or to remove people who aren't contributing. When you can't differentiate based on performance, you end up with a culture where everyone settles for "good enough." That's poison for innovation.

I understand that unions emerged to protect workers from exploitation, and that was probably necessary at one time. But in the modern economy, especially in technology, the best protection for workers is being excellent at what they do. A great engineer or designer has more job security and negotiating power than any collective bargaining agreement could provide.

What unions don't understand is that the interests of excellent employees and excellent companies are actually aligned. When we ship great products, when we create value for customers, everyone wins - shareholders, employees, and customers. But unions create an adversarial relationship that assumes the company's success comes at the expense of workers.

The best way to help workers isn't through collective bargaining - it's by creating companies that do meaningful work, that pay well, and that give people the chance to do the best work of their lives. That's a much better deal than any union contract.

Only some

The press can be incredibly valuable when journalists actually do their homework and try to understand what they're writing about. Some of the best journalists I've worked with have helped people understand not just what we're building, but why it matters and how it fits into the bigger picture.

But too much of technology journalism is lazy. Journalists write about rumors and speculation instead of actually using the products. They focus on stock prices and market share instead of asking whether something is actually good for users. They want to create drama and controversy rather than helping people understand how technology can improve their lives.

What really frustrates me is when journalists clearly haven't spent any time with a product before writing about it. They'll review the iPhone by comparing specifications to other phones, completely missing the point that it's about the total user experience. It's like reviewing a movie by counting how many actors are in it.

The press also has this obsession with inside baseball - who's fighting with whom, who's up and who's down - instead of focusing on the work itself. They'd rather write about corporate politics than about whether we're actually solving problems that matter to people.

I respect journalists who take the time to understand what they're covering and who can help the public make sense of complex issues. But unfortunately, that's a pretty small percentage of the people calling themselves technology journalists.

Only some

I have tremendous respect for medical research and the scientific basis of modern medicine. The advances we've seen in understanding the human body, developing new treatments, and extending healthy life are incredible. When you look at what medical researchers have accomplished with cancer, heart disease, and other conditions, it's clear that rigorous scientific thinking can solve problems that seemed impossible just decades ago.

But the practice of medicine - the actual delivery of healthcare - is often terrible from a user experience perspective. Hospitals are designed for the convenience of doctors and administrators, not patients. Medical records systems are fragmented and user-hostile. The whole system treats patients like they're interrupting some more important process.

I also think the medical establishment can be too rigid in its thinking sometimes. They're very good at addressing symptoms with drugs and procedures, but not always great at looking at the whole person or considering how lifestyle and environment affect health. There's room for both rigorous science and a more holistic approach to understanding what makes people healthy.

What excites me about medicine is the potential for technology to revolutionize how care is delivered. Imagine if medical devices were as intuitive as consumer electronics. Imagine if patients had access to their own data in formats they could actually understand. The intersection of technology and medicine could transform not just how we treat disease, but how we maintain health throughout our lives.

Only some

Education is one of the most important things we can do as a society, but the way most schools operate is incredibly frustrating. The potential is enormous, but the execution is often terrible. It's another example of an institution that's organized for the convenience of administrators rather than the people it's supposed to serve.

Most schools are still using an industrial model that was designed to produce workers for factories, not thinkers for the modern economy. They focus on memorization and standardized testing instead of creativity and problem-solving. They treat all students the same when we know that people learn in different ways and at different paces.

What's particularly maddening is how resistant the education establishment is to innovation. We've given away millions of computers to schools, but most teachers are still teaching the same way they did twenty years ago. They use technology as an expensive typewriter instead of recognizing how it could transform the entire learning experience.

The best teachers are incredible - they can inspire students to love learning and thinking. But the system doesn't reward excellence or allow for the kind of risk-taking that leads to breakthroughs. Instead, it rewards conformity and bureaucratic compliance.

Technology could revolutionize education, but it needs to be designed specifically for learning, not just adapted from business applications. Imagine if students could learn at their own pace, if they could access the world's knowledge instantly, if they could collaborate with peers around the globe. That's the kind of transformation education needs.

Only some

I have tremendous respect for the men and women who serve in the military - they're willing to put their lives on the line for something bigger than themselves, and that kind of commitment and sacrifice deserves our respect. The military also has a culture of discipline and mission focus that most organizations could learn from.

But like any large bureaucracy, the military can be incredibly inefficient and slow to adapt. I've seen how procurement works in the defense industry - it takes years to get approval for technology that's already obsolete by the time it's deployed. The bureaucracy often gets in the way of the mission rather than supporting it.

What's interesting about the military is that some of the most important technological breakthroughs - the internet, GPS, many advances in computing - came out of military research. When the military focuses on solving specific technical problems, they can be incredibly innovative. But when they get caught up in politics and bureaucracy, they lose that edge.

My bigger concern is when the military gets used for missions that don't really serve our national interests, or when the military-industrial complex drives policy decisions. The military should be a tool for protecting the country, not a mechanism for corporate profits or political adventures.

I respect the institution and the people who serve, but I think the military, like every other large organization, needs to constantly examine whether its structure and processes are actually serving its core mission.

Hardly any

Financial institutions represent everything that's wrong with how business is conducted today. They're obsessed with quarterly numbers instead of long-term value creation. They reward financial engineering over actual innovation. They treat companies like abstract numbers on a spreadsheet rather than organizations that solve real problems for real people.

Wall Street analysts constantly ask me about market share and margins when they should be asking whether we're building products that will still matter in ten years. They want us to maximize short-term profits by cutting R&D or shipping cheaper products, which is exactly how you destroy a company's future.

The whole financial system is built around moving money around rather than creating value. Banks make more money from trading derivatives than from helping businesses grow. Private equity firms buy companies, load them with debt, and strip out everything that made them valuable in the first place.

What really bothers me is how this short-term thinking has infected the rest of business. Too many CEOs spend their time managing stock prices instead of managing their products and customers. My approach to strategic planning starts with a simple question: What do customers really need, even if they can't articulate it yet? I don't use traditional frameworks - most of them produce mediocre, committee-designed products.

Instead, I focus on three core principles. First, radical simplicity. When I returned to Apple in 1997, we had dozens of confusing products. I cut it down to four: desktop and portable, for consumers and professionals. Innovation is saying no to 1000 things.

Second, I think in integrated ecosystems, not isolated products. The iPod wasn't just a music player - it was iPod + iTunes + Mac working seamlessly together. That's how you create real value and competitive advantage.

Third, I start with the user experience and work backward to the technology, never the other way around. Most companies start with technology and try to figure out how to sell it. We start with the customer experience and ask: what technology do we need to deliver that?

My planning process is intensely collaborative with a small group of A-players. We debate everything. We prototype relentlessly. We're not afraid to kill projects that aren't going to be insanely great. The goal isn't just to make money - it's to put something wonderful into the world.

The biggest strategic pivot I ever made was deciding to cannibalize our own iPod business with the iPhone. This was around 2004-2005, when the iPod was our cash cow - it represented 70% of our revenue and was growing like crazy.

But I could see the writing on the wall. Cell phones were getting smarter and starting to play music. I realized that eventually, someone was going to put the iPod out of business. I said to the team: "Let's make sure it's us."

Everyone thought I was insane. The iPod was printing money. Why would we risk killing it with an unproven product? But that's exactly why we had to do it. When you're ahead, that's when you have the luxury to take big risks.

The decision was driven by three factors: First, I could see convergence coming - people didn't want to carry multiple devices. Second, we had built incredible competency in user interface design that could revolutionize phones. Third, I fundamentally believed that the best products come from taking big leaps, not incremental improvements.

The scariest part wasn't the technology - it was convincing our retail partners and investors that we were going to potentially destroy our most successful product. But that's what real innovation requires. You can't be afraid to cannibalize yourself, because if you don't, someone else will.

I fundamentally reject the premise that there's always a tension between short-term and long-term. The best way to deliver great short-term results is to be obsessively focused on the long-term.

Wall Street analysts constantly pressured us to maximize quarterly earnings, cut R&D, license our technology to competitors - basically do everything that would destroy Apple's future for a temporary stock bump. I ignored them completely. If you optimize for quarterly results, you'll build mediocre products and eventually lose.

My approach is simple: Build insanely great products, and the financial results will follow. Sometimes that means spending billions on unproven technologies like the original iPhone touchscreen. Sometimes it means saying no to easy revenue opportunities that would dilute our brand.

When we launched the first iMac, it would have been much cheaper to use a standard beige box. But we invested in translucent colored plastics that cost significantly more and took months to perfect. Short-term, it hurt our margins. Long-term, it completely redefined what computers could look like and feel like.

The key is having enough financial strength to make these long-term bets. When you're successful, that's exactly when you should be taking the biggest risks and making the boldest investments. Success gives you the luxury to think 5-10 years ahead instead of just next quarter.

Most companies die because they optimize for the short-term when they should be preparing for the future.

I have a very different approach to competitive analysis than most companies. Most CEOs obsess over their competitors' features and try to copy them. I study competitors to understand what NOT to do.

I personally tear apart every major competitor product. I want to understand their design philosophy, their manufacturing approach, their cost structure. This gives me insight into their limitations and blind spots.

But here's the key difference: I don't use this intelligence to build better versions of their products. I use it to build completely different products that make theirs obsolete. When everyone was making faster MP3 players, we built the iPod. When everyone was making smartphones with keyboards, we built the iPhone with a touchscreen.

Traditional market research is mostly useless. Focus groups will tell you to make incremental improvements to existing products. People don't know what they want until you show it to them. Henry Ford's customers would have asked for faster horses.

My real competitive intelligence comes from understanding technology trends 3-5 years ahead and asking: what becomes possible when this technology matures? That's where real opportunities hide - in the gap between what's technically possible and what customers think they need.

The decision to launch Apple Stores is a perfect example. Every retail expert told us we were insane - computer companies don't do retail, especially premium retail. Gateway had just closed their stores. The data seemed to support their pessimism.

I analyzed successful retail models - particularly luxury retailers like Tiffany and Bang & Olufsen. The data showed that premium brands with experiential products needed their own retail environment to capture full value. Their revenue per square foot was 3-5x higher than traditional computer retailers.

We also gathered detailed analytics on customer behavior in existing stores. People would spend 2-3 minutes with our products in CompUSA, but 15-20 minutes when they had proper demonstrations. Purchase intent jumped from 15% to 60% with extended engagement.

The breakthrough insight came from analyzing our service data. Customers who received quality technical support had 40% higher lifetime value and were 3x more likely to buy additional products. But third-party retailers provided terrible support.

So the data told a clear story: we needed to control the entire customer experience from discovery to purchase to support. We opened our first stores in high-traffic, premium locations and measured everything obsessively - traffic patterns, conversion rates, product interaction time, genius bar utilization.

The results validated the strategy: our revenue per square foot became the highest in retail.

The Intel transition is a good example. Moving from PowerPC to Intel processors was incredibly risky - it could break software compatibility and alienate our developer community. For the unknowns - customer reception, developer adoption, competitive response - I relied on our track record with the iPod and Mac. We understood how to create desire for premium products and build developer ecosystems.

The key insight was that waiting for certainty is itself a decision - usually the wrong one. If you wait until the market is proven, you're too late. You have to be willing to bet on your team's ability to execute and solve problems as they emerge.

Perfect information doesn't exist for breakthrough innovations. You make the best decision you can with available data, then execute flawlessly to prove yourself right.

Third, choose partners based on character and shared values, not just talent.

When I returned to Apple in 1997, I applied these lessons. I restructured the board, maintained clear authority over product decisions, and built an executive team with people I trusted completely - Jonathan Ive, Tim Cook, people who shared our mission.

That painful experience taught me that leadership isn't just about vision and execution - it's about power, politics, and human nature.
