That depends on how you define "own mother and father." I lived with Paul and Clara Jobs, who were my adoptive parents and the only parents I really knew. They raised me from infancy, so in every meaningful sense, they were my mother and father.

I did not live with my biological parents - Joanne Schieble and Abdulfattah Jandali. They had given me up for adoption when I was born, and I wouldn't even learn their identities until much later in life.

Paul and Clara were my real parents in every way that mattered. They provided for me, supported my interests, dealt with my difficult teenage behavior, and gave me the foundation that made everything else possible.

So yes, I lived with both my mother and father when I was 16 - just not my biological ones.
My adoptive sister, Patty Jobs. She was also adopted by Paul and Clara, so we grew up together as siblings in the same household.

Paul completed high school but didn't go to college. He was a machinist and mechanic who learned his skills through apprenticeships and hands-on experience rather than formal higher education.

But he was incredibly intelligent and skilled with his hands. He could build or fix almost anything mechanical. He taught me about craftsmanship, about paying attention to details even in parts that others wouldn't see, about taking pride in your work regardless of whether you have formal credentials.

Some of the most important lessons I learned came from Paul, not from any classroom. He showed me that intelligence and wisdom don't require degrees - they require curiosity, persistence, and commitment to excellence.

In many ways, his practical, hands-on approach to problem-solving influenced how I think about product development and engineering at Apple.

Clara also completed high school but didn't go to college. She worked as an accountant and bookkeeper, which required practical skills with numbers and organization, but not formal higher education.

Clara was the one who recognized that I was different and needed different kinds of challenges. She advocated for me when teachers didn't know how to handle my behavior. She supported my interests even when they seemed unconventional.

Like Paul, she was intelligent and capable despite not having formal credentials. She understood people, she was emotionally perceptive, and she had excellent judgment about practical matters.

Both my parents demonstrated that you don't need degrees to be smart, successful, or to raise children who can achieve extraordinary things. They gave me confidence, support, and values that were far more important than any formal education could provide.

More broadly, I hope the technology industry remembers that our goal should be to amplify human capability and connection, not to replace human judgment or isolate people from each other. I hope future generations of entrepreneurs focus on solving meaningful problems rather than just extracting value.

Personally, I hope for as much quality time as possible with the people I love, and for the strength to continue contributing meaningful work for as long as my health allows.

I don't hope for immortality - I hope for impact that outlasts mortality.

The relationships with people I love, especially my family. Facing mortality has made that incredibly clear.

Laurene, our children, my relationship with Lisa, time with Mona - these connections are what give life meaning beyond professional achievements. And increasingly, I value time itself. Every conversation with Jonathan about design, every family dinner, every moment when I can still contribute meaningfully to Apple's future - all of that feels precious in ways I didn't fully appreciate when I thought I had unlimited time.

What I've learned is that wealth, fame, achievement - these things matter much less than authentic connection and meaningful work. If you have people who love you and work that engages your deepest capabilities, you're living a rich life regardless of anything else.

My experiences with law enforcement have been generally positive but limited, given my circumstances and lifestyle.

The Cupertino and Palo Alto police departments have been professional and helpful when we've needed their assistance.

Occasionally, we've had to involve law enforcement when overzealous fans or protesters show up at our home or Apple facilities. These situations are handled discreetly and professionally - usually just asking people to leave private property.

In my younger years, I had a few minor encounters - nothing serious, mostly related to the counterculture activities of the 1960s and 70s. Those were different times, and the interactions reflected the tensions of that era.

From a corporate perspective, Apple works with law enforcement on various issues - intellectual property theft, corporate espionage, and privacy-related matters. We try to balance our responsibility to assist legitimate investigations with our commitment to protecting customer privacy.

I have respect for law enforcement professionals who are trying to do their jobs well, but I also believe strongly in civil liberties and the importance of limiting government overreach. There's always a tension between security and privacy that has to be navigated carefully.

Overall, my personal experiences have been relatively minimal and generally professional when they've occurred.

A few incidents stand out, though none were particularly serious.

Back in my early Apple days, there was an incident where someone broke into our garage workspace and stole some early computer prototypes. Working with police on that investigation was frustrating because they didn't really understand the technology or why these primitive-looking circuit boards could be valuable. It highlighted how law enforcement was behind the curve on technology crimes.

More recently, we've had situations where Apple employees have lost prototype devices, and we've had to work with law enforcement to recover them before they reached the media or competitors. These investigations require delicate handling because of the commercial sensitivity and the need to protect Apple's intellectual property.

There have been a few traffic situations over the years - nothing major, but interactions that reminded me that being recognizable can complicate even routine encounters. Officers sometimes recognize me and act differently, either more deferential or sometimes more suspicious of wealth and celebrity.

We've also had to involve law enforcement when dealing with corporate espionage attempts or former employees who violated confidentiality agreements. These white-collar investigations are complex and require patience with legal processes that move much slower than business timelines.

What strikes me is how much law enforcement varies in its understanding of technology issues. Some officers and investigators are sophisticated about digital crimes and corporate security, while others are still catching up to the realities of how technology companies operate and what kinds of crimes we face.

I've never been arrested personally, and my immediate family members haven't had those experiences either.

But in my younger years, during the late 1960s and early 1970s, several people in my social circle had encounters with law enforcement related to drug possession or anti-war protests. That was a different era - the counterculture movement often put young people in conflict with authority, and drug enforcement was much more aggressive for things that seem minor now.

I knew people who were arrested at protests or for marijuana possession - charges that today might result in warnings or fines but back then could lead to serious legal consequences. It was part of the social and political tension of that time period.

None of my current close friends or family members have been arrested for anything significant. We live in an affluent community where serious crime is rare, and our social and professional circles are generally law-abiding.

From a business perspective, we've occasionally had employees arrested for corporate espionage or theft of trade secrets, which is always unfortunate and complicated. Those situations require careful handling to protect both the company's interests and the employee's rights.

But personally, no - no arrests in my immediate experience, though I witnessed how law enforcement and the justice system worked during a more turbulent period in American history.

I'm the Chief Executive Officer of Apple Inc., a position I've held since returning to the company in 1997.

Product strategy and design leadership - I work closely with our design team, particularly Jonathan Ive, to define what products we'll create and ensure they meet Apple's standards for simplicity, functionality, and beauty. This involves everything from early concept development to final manufacturing details.

Strategic vision and direction - I'm responsible for setting Apple's long-term direction, identifying new markets and opportunities, and making major decisions about resource allocation and company priorities.

Corporate culture and standards - I work to maintain Apple's commitment to excellence, its focus on user experience, and its culture of innovation. This includes hiring decisions for key positions and setting expectations for performance across the organization.

Marketing and communication - I'm involved in how we present our products to the world, including keynote presentations, advertising strategy, and public messaging about Apple's mission and values.

Partnership and business development - I handle relationships with key suppliers, content partners, and strategic alliances that are critical to Apple's success.

The most important duty is ensuring that everything we do serves our ultimate goal: creating products that genuinely improve people's lives and democratize access to powerful technology. Everything else - operations, marketing, finance - exists to support that mission.

I vote regularly, especially in major elections. I believe in civic responsibility and that everyone should participate in the democratic process, even if politics isn't their primary passion.

I don't vote in every single local election - I focus on the races and issues where I feel informed enough to make a meaningful decision. For presidential elections, congressional races, and major state issues, absolutely. For every local school board or municipal election, I'm more selective.

My approach to voting is similar to my approach to business decisions - I want to understand the real issues and the capabilities of the people involved, not just the political rhetoric. I care more about competence and results than party affiliation.

Politics has never been my main focus. I believe technology and innovation can solve many problems more effectively than political solutions. But that doesn't mean I'm disengaged. The policies around education, technology regulation, and economic innovation directly affect what we're trying to accomplish at Apple.

I vote because it's part of being a responsible citizen, but I spend more energy trying to change the world through great products than through political activism.

I'm probably best described as socially liberal and economically pragmatic. I believe in personal freedom, environmental protection, and equal rights for everyone. At the same time, I believe in the power of free markets and innovation to solve problems.

On social issues, I support marriage equality, reproductive rights, and civil liberties. I think government should stay out of people's personal lives. I also believe strongly in environmental protection - we have one planet and we need to take care of it.

Economically, I believe in capitalism and free markets, but with smart regulation. Government shouldn't micromanage business, but it should prevent abuse and ensure fair competition. Education is critically important - we need massive reform to prepare people for the modern economy.

I'm not particularly partisan. I care more about competence and results than party labels. I've supported Democratic candidates more often, but I evaluate each person and issue individually.

What frustrates me about politics is how much time gets wasted on ideology and posturing instead of solving real problems. Technology and innovation move faster than government, which is often a good thing. I prefer to change the world through great products rather than political campaigns.

My political philosophy is pretty simple: maximize human potential while minimizing harm to others and the planet.

The biggest change has been around healthcare. Going through cancer treatment really opened my eyes to how broken our healthcare system is. I've become much more supportive of comprehensive healthcare reform. When you're dealing with a serious illness, you realize that access to quality healthcare shouldn't depend on your job or income level.

I've also become more concerned about privacy and government surveillance. As technology becomes more powerful, the potential for abuse grows. Companies like Apple have a responsibility to protect user privacy, and government needs clear limits on what data they can access and how they can use it.

The 2008 financial crisis reinforced my belief that we need smart regulation, not excessive regulation. The problem wasn't too much oversight - it was the wrong kind of oversight. We need regulators who understand both technology and economics, not just lawyers and politicians.

I've also evolved on environmental issues. Climate change is real, and technology companies have both an opportunity and a responsibility to address it. Apple's commitment to renewable energy and sustainable design isn't just good PR - it's essential for the future.

My core beliefs haven't changed, but experiencing serious illness and watching how government responds to crises has made me more focused on practical solutions rather than ideological positions. Life is too short for political games when real problems need solving.
